questions.q: What does the `@api` decorator mark a field or method as?
options: Part of the component's public interface, settable or readable by a parent component
A field that is automatically encrypted in transit
A field that can never be changed after the component is created
A method that runs automatically on every re-render
questions.explain: `@api` marks a property or method as part of a component's public API, meaning a parent component is allowed to set or read it (or call it, for a method).

questions.q: In `<c-contact-card record-id={selectedId}></c-contact-card>`, why is the attribute written as `record-id` instead of `recordId`?
options: HTML attributes in LWC markup use kebab-case even though the matching class property is camelCase
It's a typo; LWC requires the attribute to exactly match the camelCase property name
Kebab-case is only required for `@track` properties, not `@api` properties
The attribute name has no relationship to the property name at all
questions.explain: Markup attributes use kebab-case, while the matching class property stays camelCase -- this is why `recordId` in the class becomes `record-id` in the parent's template.

questions.q: Since the Spring '20 release, which fields are reactive automatically, with no decorator required?
options: No fields are reactive without a decorator; `@track` is always required
Only fields decorated with `@api`
Any class field referenced in the template or a getter, when the field itself is reassigned to a new value
Only fields that hold primitive numbers, never strings or booleans
questions.explain: Simple reassignment of a class field referenced in the template (directly or via a getter) is observed automatically since Spring '20, with no decorator needed -- `@track` is not required just to pick up a new value being assigned to a field.

questions.q: In this lesson's `address` example, why does `this.address.city = event.target.value;` need `@track` (or a different approach) to be observed, while `this.count = this.count + 1;` does not?
options: Because strings are never reactive in LWC, only numbers are
Because the first example mutates a property inside an existing object, while the second reassigns the whole field to a new value -- only the latter is automatically observed
Because `address` is an `@api` property and `count` is not
There is no real difference; both require `@track` to work correctly
questions.explain: Reassigning a field to a brand-new value (like `this.count = this.count + 1`) is automatically observed. Mutating a property inside an existing object or array in place is not automatically observed unless the field is decorated with `@track`, or unless you reassign the whole object/array instead (e.g. with the spread operator).

questions.q: What is the rule of thumb this lesson gives for deciding whether a property should be `@api`?
options: Every field in a component should be marked `@api` by default, for consistency
If a value is configured by or communicated to a parent component (or Lightning App Builder), it should be `@api`; purely internal rendering state should stay a plain internal field
Only boolean fields should ever be marked `@api`
`@api` should only be used on methods, never on fields
questions.explain: The lesson's rule of thumb ties `@api` to the component's public contract: values a parent or App Builder configures or reads should be `@api`; purely internal bookkeeping should stay internal to keep the component's interface clean.
